title: Why Your Navigation Stinks
intro: People search for information the way animals forage for food. They follow a trail of clues about what lies ahead — **information scent**. Navigation fails when labels stop giving off scent.

learn.title: Information foraging
learn.text:
Pirolli and Card's information foraging theory: users follow clues that suggest what content or action lies ahead.

None of this is new. Information scent is a framing for principles you already know — starting with Nielsen's *match between system and the real world*, or as Calabro puts it: **talk like a human, not a product manager**.

options: The clues that suggest what lies behind a link
The visual weight given to key navigation items
The time it takes users to find a page
A ranking of pages by how often they are visited
try.explain: Users predict where their goal lives, then follow the trail.

learn.title: Where scent goes to die
learn.text:
Bad scent is usually the result of compromise, not sabotage: a label rewritten for a marketing push, a category renamed after the org chart.

• **Vague labels** — “Explore”, “Solutions”, “Resources”, “Experience”
• **Icons without text** — a gear or lightning bolt is a guessing game
• **Overlapping categories** — “Help Center”, “Support Articles” and “FAQs” side by side
• **Branded language** that doesn't match user vocabulary
• **Org-chart IA**

try.q: A site has “Help Center”, “Support Articles” and “FAQs” in the same menu. What's the problem?
options: Overlapping categories give no clear trail
Three links is too many for a help section
Support content should live behind login
The labels are too long for a top nav
try.explain: Users can't predict which one holds their answer.

learn.title: How to spot it and fix it
learn.text:
**Spot it:** tree tests and card sorts, 5-second tests, click tracking, and quotes from usability tests like “I wouldn't have clicked that.”

**Fix it:** plain language that matches what users search for; key tasks visible from the main entry points; combine or rename categories that are too similar; add short explanatory text; and if you use icons, always pair them with labels.

try.q: Which method tells you whether users can predict what a section contains?
options: A tree test
A/B testing two layouts
A satisfaction survey
A heuristic review by two experts
try.explain: Tree tests and card sorts check the IA against user expectations.

options: Pirolli and Card's
Nielsen and Norman's
Pirolli and Nielsen's
Card and Moran's
test.explain: They studied how people search for information the way animals forage.

test.q: Why do labels usually lose their scent?
options: Through compromise, not bad intent
Because designers prefer short words
Because translations lose meaning
Because analytics reward clever names
test.explain: A marketing rewrite here, an org-chart rename there.

test.q: What is wrong with “Explore” as a top-level label?
options: It gives no clue what's behind it
It is too informal for enterprise products
It duplicates the search function
It performs poorly on small screens
test.explain: Vague labels are the first category of scent failure.

test.q: What does a 5-second test tell you here?
options: Whether users can say what a section is about
How long the page takes to load
Which link gets the most clicks
Whether the layout works on mobile
test.explain: It checks whether the label and context communicate quickly.

test.q: Why is “scent” a useful word with stakeholders?
options: It explains that users are following clues, not failing
It sounds more scientific than usability
It avoids blaming the marketing team
It maps directly to analytics metrics
test.explain: It gives non-UX colleagues language for what is going wrong.
